Journal of Statistical Software:
http://dx.doi.org/10.18637/jss.v090.i02. Please, use this reference
for citations.

There's also a new version (v4.3.0) on CRAN. Special thanks to Tom

list of changes: https://r-simmer.org/news/index.html#simmer-4-3-0

Regards,
--
Iñaki Úcar

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Electric Car Charging Simulator
messages.subject_clean: [simmer-devel] Electric Car Charging Simulator
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your answer - now there are some details, I'm struggling with. I want to have a pre-defined number of cars in the simulation and the remaining battery when they leave the charger should be handed over to the new arrival that starts charging. And I have a problem, that I can't always start at midnight, because some car-trips leap into the next day:

My solution so far:

I generate a fixed number of cars all at time zero, I infinitely rollback the trajectory until the run ends, e.g. after a year in the simulation.

As my simulator should work with real-life data, I should sample from a dataset (sample attached) rather than use approximated functions.

If every household would only do a single trip per day, I could randomly sample from the dataset, but as most households do more than one trip per day (e.g. see car2 in the image above), this does not work for me.

So I wrote a function multiple_days that predefines the full-year in terms of when at home, when driving and how far. I use a closure timeout_generator that is initialized with data to run the full simulation duration and every time it is called, it returns when the next trip starts and how long it will last.

 timeout_generator <- function(){
   s <- force(multiple_days())
   i <- 0
   function(){
     i <<- i + 1
     return(slice(s,i))
   }
 }

This works great for a single car in the simulation, but if I have more than one car, than both cars share the closure. I don't know how multiple arrivals can call their specific closure, so that each closure has its own R-environment.

So I came up with a very ugly for-loop that initializes an array of closures
array <- c()
newValues <- function() {timeout_generator}
for (i in seq(1,cars)){
   array <- append(array,newValues()())
}

env %>%
   add_resource("Charger", cars) %>%
   add_generator("Car", trajectory, mon=2, at(rep(0,cars))) %>% run(24*60*days)

Inside the trajectory, I update the attributes based on the array element that is assigned to the car.

Two problems:
1) Initializing the closure outside of the trajectory prevents me to use the nice tools for replication of the simulation - any ideas?
2) Even when I keep today's architecture, and build a for-loop around the whole closure-array-initialization and env-execution , after some hundred repetitions the closure timeout_generator returns no more meaningful values. No clue.

I guess, I need to rewrite the overall structure?

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 3 Aug 2019 at 11:23, Benjamin Sawicki
<ihrproje...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you for your answer - now there are some details, I'm struggling with. I want to have a pre-defined number of cars in the simulation and the remaining battery when they leave the charger should be handed over to the new arrival that starts charging. And I have a problem, that I can't always start at midnight, because some car-trips leap into the next day:
>
>

> My solution so far:
>
> I generate a fixed number of cars all at time zero, I infinitely rollback the trajectory until the run ends, e.g. after a year in the simulation.
>
> As my simulator should work with real-life data, I should sample from a dataset (sample attached) rather than use approximated functions.
>
> If every household would only do a single trip per day, I could randomly sample from the dataset, but as most households do more than one trip per day (e.g. see car2 in the image above), this does not work for me.

Your dataset covers a day or a full year? Are different trip numbers
for the same household_nr in the same day?

Longitudinal data is tricky. You could take a look at resampling
methodologies for this kind of data such as cluster bootstrapping or
hierarchical resampling. The idea is that you should sample
household_nrs, not individual rows (and also days, if you have a whole
year). E.g., packages rsample and fabricatr have helpers for this.

Another idea would be to write a data generator that recreates various
statistics in your dataset: autocorrelations, distribution of
distances, distribution of trip durations conditioned to the distance,
distributions of weights and number of trips maybe also conditioned to
other statistics...

Either way, if you manage to resample/simulate your data to produce N
datasets, it would be easy to feed them into simmer using
add_dataframe. See https://www.enchufa2.es/archives/simmer-3-8-0.html

> So I wrote a function multiple_days that predefines the full-year in terms of when at home, when driving and how far. I use a closure timeout_generator that is initialized with data to run the full simulation duration and every time it is called, it returns when the next trip starts and how long it will last.
>

> This works great for a single car in the simulation, but if I have more than one car, than both cars share the closure. I don't know how multiple arrivals can call their specific closure, so that each closure has its own R-environment.
>
> So I came up with a very ugly for-loop that initializes an array of closures

Another solution would be to set s and i as vectors and index them
inside the closure instead of indexing a list of closures. But I mean,
the list of closures is just fine. It's a bit ugly only because you
are using a loop instead of lapply. :)

> Two problems:
> 1) Initializing the closure outside of the trajectory prevents me to use the nice tools for replication of the simulation - any ideas?

I tend to write a function that contains the whole simulation (except,
maybe, for some constants), and then I replicate that. That's how it's
done in all the scenarios in this vignette:
https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g

> 2) Even when I keep today's architecture, and build a for-loop around the whole closure-array-initialization and env-execution , after some hundred repetitions the closure timeout_generator returns no more meaningful values. No clue.

My guess, something related to reference semantics. Take a look at
this question and my answer:
https://stackoverflow.com/q/57319358/6788081

Again, the methodology above (encapsulating everything in a function)
solves all this kind of issues.

> I guess, I need to rewrite the overall structure?

I think it's fine. Unless you figure out how to resample/simulate your
data as discussed above (and it shouldn't be very different to what
multiple_days does now).

Iñaki

Hi.

I have a model that simulates costs and health-related benefits across 8+ interventions. For each intervention, the model simulates around ten thousand patients in a run, and must run 1000 times.

I have tried to use several parallel processing packages but keep running into errors that I can't understand.

Can you please write a short chunk of code that could help me understand how to implement this in my model?

Also, because I am running the exact model for all 8 Interventions, I am using a for loop that controls the intervention being modelled with reset() and run() inside the loop. This is working fine and I am getting the expected results. Is there a better way?

Your help is much appreciated.

Thank you.
Wael

messages.body_plain:
Parallel processing on R is a challenge on Windows due to lack of fork() - but a lot easier on Linux, or using the Windows Linux Subsystem.

If you're using Linux/WSL then my approach has been to create a wrapper around the simmer environment and use mclapply(). I think one of the vignettes shows a method.

I do have a working method on Windows too but it's a bit more involved as you have to set up a cluster and pull all the libraries / environment over.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
This is what I'm using on Windows:

library("doParallel") registerDoParallel(cores=8) trials<-4 envs <- foreach(icount(trials), .combine=c, .noexport=c("gen_emergency_patients","gen_elective_patients"),.export=c("progress_bar"), .packages=c("dplyr","bizdays","Rcpp","simmer"), .verbose=TRUE) %dopar% { simmer_wrapper(1) }

Where simmer_wrapper is a function that contains all the trajectory definitions and associated functions, and finishes with :

env %>%
     run(until=1622312575 ) %>%
     wrap()

It's not the greatest solution as it effectively sets up 8 totally independent R instances, and each has to load all the libraries and do the setup etc (eg I had to move bizday's calendar initialising into the wrapper loop rather than with mclapply where it could be initialised once at the start)

I've installed WSL Ubuntu on Windows 10 and using rstudio-server on there it works fine with mclapply(), and is all a lot easier to understand. The only reason I bothered to work out a Windows solution was because I've been offered use of a 24-core Xeon running Windows. If you have the choice I'd definitely go for Linux or WSL.

Tom

I think this is the guide I used :

https://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/2017/12/r-in-the-windows-subsystem-for-linux.html

Basically installed Ubuntu WSL via the Windows Store, then installed rstudio-server on that. You don't need the GUI as rstudio is basically a webpage anyway (I think it uses Firefox). So I just open my Ubuntu prompt, launch rstudio-server from there, and use my normal Windows browser to connect to rstudio-server (http://localhost:8787/).

Only real advantage is for much easier parallel processing, but for me the speedup is very handy. Although there is quite a long delay after the simmer simulations finish running before the results are available (presumably the environments being brought back together).

Tom

On Sun, 25 Aug 2019 at 20:19, Tom Lawton <t...@t-lawton.org> wrote:
>
> This is what I'm using on Windows:
>

> library("doParallel") ...

You may want to try the future.apply package [1]. Its future_lapply
function is a drop-in replacement for lapply and mclapply, and you
just need to set the plan to multiprocess: if multicore is available
(Linux and Mac), it runs in multicore mode; if not (Windows), it runs
in multiprocess mode (just what you are doing with doParallel, but the
easy way).

Also, if you have some cluster available at some point, you can
distribute your simulations in that cluster again just by changing the
plan. No further changes to the code are needed.

Iñaki

[1] https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/future.apply/vignettes/future.apply-1-overview.html

>
> I have already tried future_lapply but it couldn't export the simmer-created environment to the other sessions.

Because the simulation environment is a C++ object, and this cannot be
exported. Instead, as Tom suggested, the best way is to wrap the whole
simulation in function (including all the code setting up trajectories
and the simulation environment), and run this function in the workers,
as [1] demonstrates.

[1] https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-aa-5g

Iñaki
